caption: Tropospheric ducting. A temperature inversion - warm air over cool surface air - traps VHF and UHF signals against the surface and carries them far beyond the normal horizon, over water and over land, for hundreds of miles. Microwave ducts form over large bodies of water with a typical range of 100 to 300 miles; the high-pressure inversion weather that builds them is the 'lift' operators watch for.
spoken: A cross-section of a tropospheric duct. Aloft, a dashed double line marks a temperature inversion - warm air sitting over cool surface air. From the transmitter at the left, one dashed ray at a steeper angle passes through the layer and escapes to space: that is what happens without an inversion. The ducted ray, launched at a shallow angle, bends over beneath the inversion, returns to the surface, reflects, and bends over again - trapped between the surface and the layer, hopping along over a large body of water in the middle of the path and over land beyond it, until it reaches a receiver hundreds of miles away, far past the normal horizon. A circled H marks the high-pressure weather behind it: inversion weather is the 'lift' VHF operators watch for. The exam pins microwave ducts forming over large bodies of water, with a typical range of 100 to 300 miles.
